analogy.p: A balanced equation is a recipe: 'one cake needs 2 eggs and 1 bag of flour'. The balancing numbers give you the ratio of items, not their weights. If you have 10 eggs but only 3 bags of flour, you can make only 3 cakes: flour is the limiting ingredient and the leftover eggs are the excess. The number of cakes is decided by the limiting ingredient, just as the amount of product is decided by the limiting reactant. The analogy breaks down because ingredients can be bought in any units, whereas in chemistry you must convert grams into moles using Mr before comparing amounts.
analogy.t: The recipe and the shopping basket

bullets: In 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO, the ratio is **2 mol Mg : 1 mol O2 : 2 mol MgO**.
Balancing numbers multiply everything that follows them: 2MgO means 2 Mg atoms and 2 O atoms; 2Al2O3 contains 4 Al and 6 O.
Small numbers inside formulae (subscripts) are part of the substance and must **never** be changed when balancing; only balancing numbers can be altered.
The ratio of particles equals the ratio of moles, because one mole of any substance contains the same number of particles (6.02 × 10²³).
State symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq) show the physical state; (aq) means dissolved in water.
The ratio of masses is found only after converting moles to grams using Mr: mass = moles × Mr.
A reaction equation represents the *smallest whole-number ratio*; real experiments can use any multiple of it.
core.h: What a balanced symbol equation tells you
core.p: A **balanced symbol equation** shows the **formulae of the reactants and products** and has the **same number of atoms of each element on both sides**, because atoms are never created or destroyed in a chemical reaction. The big numbers written in front of formulae, called **balancing numbers** (or coefficients), tell you the **ratio of the amounts (in moles) of each substance**. They do **not** tell you the ratio of the masses. This is the single most important idea in reacting-mass calculations: equations work in moles, but in the lab you weigh grams.

bullets: Total mass of reactants = total mass of products (in a **closed system** where nothing can enter or escape).
Check: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO: reactants 48 g + 32 g = 80 g; product 2 × 40 g = 80 g. ✓
Check: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2: 100 g → 56 g + 44 g = 100 g ✓.
The *number of atoms* is conserved, so the balanced equation is the evidence that mass is conserved.
Mass appears to change only when a gas enters or leaves an **open container**; this is not a breakdown of the law (see the section on apparent mass changes).
Examiners reward the phrase 'no atoms are lost or made' when explaining conservation of mass.
Link: conservation of mass is the basis of percentage yield and atom economy calculations.
core.h: Conservation of mass and why it makes calculations possible
core.p: The **law of conservation of mass** states that **no atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction, so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants**. This is why we can predict the mass of a product from the mass of a reactant. When you add up the masses of all the reactants (using moles × Mr) you must get the same total as for all the products. This gives you a powerful check on your arithmetic: if the totals do not match, you have made a mistake somewhere.

bullets: moles (mol) = mass (g) ÷ Mr; mass (g) = moles × Mr; Mr = mass ÷ moles.
Use the Ar values given in the question or on the periodic table: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Mg 24, Al 27, S 32, Cl 35.5, K 39, Ca 40, Fe 56, Cu 63.5, Zn 65.
Brackets multiply everything inside: Ca(NO3)2 has 1 Ca, 2 N, 6 O, so Mr = 40 + 28 + 96 = 164.
Hydrated salts: CuSO4·5H2O has Mr = 63.5 + 32 + 64 + 5 × 18 = 249.5.
Always show the Mr working: examiners give a mark for a correct Mr.
Keep the full calculator display until the final answer and only then round; Cl is 35.5, not 35 or 36.
If the mass is given in kg or tonnes, convert to grams first (1 kg = 1000 g; 1 tonne = 1 000 000 g).
core.h: Relative formula mass and moles: the tools you need
core.p: Every reacting-mass calculation uses two tools. First, the **relative formula mass (Mr)** is found by adding up the relative atomic masses (Ar, from the periodic table) of all atoms in the formula, e.g. Mr of Mg(OH)2 = 24 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 58. Second, the **mole** links mass and Mr: **moles = mass ÷ Mr**, with mass in **grams** and the answer in **mol**. You can rearrange this to **mass = moles × Mr** and **Mr = mass ÷ moles**. The balancing numbers then convert moles of one substance into moles of another.

bullets: Step 1: balanced equation, e.g. 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO.
Step 2: moles of known = mass ÷ Mr (e.g. 6.0 g Mg ÷ 24 = 0.25 mol).
Step 3: use the ratio: 2 mol Mg gives 2 mol MgO, so 0.25 mol Mg gives 0.25 mol MgO.
Step 4: mass of wanted = moles × Mr (0.25 × 40 = 10.0 g MgO).
Only the **ratio between the two substances you are interested in** matters; ignore every other substance in the equation.
The same method works backwards: to find the mass of reactant needed for a target mass of product, go from product moles to reactant moles.
Include units at each step (g, mol) and a unit in the final answer; omitting the unit often loses the last mark.
core.h: The four-step method for calculating a reacting mass (Higher tier)
core.p: Almost every question that asks for the mass of a product or a reactant follows the same pattern, and using it every time stops you losing marks. **Step 1:** write the balanced equation. **Step 2:** convert the mass of the *known* substance to **moles** (mass ÷ Mr). **Step 3:** use the **balancing numbers** to find the moles of the *wanted* substance. **Step 4:** convert those moles to **mass** (moles × Mr). Setting the working out as four short lines also lets an examiner give 'error carried forward' marks if one slip occurs early on.

bullets: Reacting masses are Mr × balancing number for each substance.
Scale factor = mass you have ÷ mass in the equation (6.0 ÷ 48 = 0.125).
Wanted mass = scale factor × mass of wanted substance in the equation (0.125 × 80 = 10 g).
This is just the moles method with the arithmetic done in a different order, so it is equally valid in an exam.
If asked to show your working, a clear ratio line scores method marks as long as the Mr values are visible.
Use the shortcut to estimate answers: the product mass should be sensible relative to the reactant mass.
The shortcut is especially quick for 'how much from 1 tonne' industrial questions.
core.h: Using the ratio of masses as a shortcut
core.p: Once you understand the moles method, you can use the **reacting-mass ratio** as a quicker alternative. Work out the mass of each substance in the equation by multiplying its Mr by its balancing number, then scale up or down by the same factor. For 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO, 2 × 24 = **48 g of Mg** reacts to make 2 × 40 = **80 g of MgO**. If you only have 6.0 g of Mg, that is 48 ÷ 8, so the product is 80 ÷ 8 = **10.0 g**. Both methods must give the same answer, so you can use one to check the other.

bullets: Thermal decomposition: 25 g CaCO3 (Mr 100) = 0.25 mol → 0.25 mol CaO = 14 g and 0.25 mol CO2 = 11 g (14 + 11 = 25 g ✓).
Metal + acid: 6.5 g Zn (Ar 65) = 0.10 mol → 0.10 mol H2 = 0.20 g (Mr 2) and 0.10 mol ZnCl2 = 13.6 g (Mr 136).
Reduction of iron(III) oxide: 160 g Fe2O3 (Mr 160) = 1.00 mol → 2.00 mol Fe = 112 g.
Combustion: methane CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O; 16 g CH4 (1 mol) needs 2 mol O2 = 64 g.
Precipitation: Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ react 1:1, so equal moles of AgNO3 and NaCl give the maximum AgCl.
Neutralisation: H2SO4 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2H2O, so 1 mol acid reacts with 2 mol alkali.
Electrolysis of Al2O3: 2Al2O3 → 4Al + 3O2; 204 g (2 mol) Al2O3 gives 108 g Al.
core.h: Worked pattern for common reaction types
core.p: The same method applies to every type of reaction in the specification. In **thermal decomposition** (CaCO3 → CaO + CO2) one reactant gives two products, so the ratio is 1:1:1. In **metal + acid** reactions (Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2) you must pay attention to the 2 in front of HCl. In **reduction of metal oxides** (Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2) the ratio is 1:3:2:3 so the moles of iron are twice the moles of iron(III) oxide. Always read the *balancing numbers* for your two substances and use only those.

bullets: Step 1: convert each mass to moles (mass ÷ Mr).
Step 2: divide each by the smallest number of moles to get a ratio.
Step 3: if needed, multiply to remove fractions (e.g. 1 : 1.5 : 1 becomes 2 : 3 : 2).
Step 4: write the equation with those balancing numbers in front of the correct formulae.
Example: 5.4 g Al (0.20 mol) + 21.3 g Cl2 (0.30 mol) → 26.7 g AlCl3 (0.20 mol) gives 0.20 : 0.30 : 0.20 = 2 : 3 : 2, so 2Al + 3Cl2 → 2AlCl3.
Check by adding: reactants 5.4 + 21.3 = 26.7 g = mass of product, so mass is conserved.
Remember to use the correct formula for each substance, e.g. chlorine is Cl2 (Mr 71), not Cl.
core.h: Using moles to balance equations from masses (Higher tier)
core.p: If you are given the masses of the reactants and products, you can **work out the balancing numbers** by converting each mass to moles and finding the simplest whole-number ratio. Divide all the mole values by the **smallest** one, and if the results are not whole numbers, multiply them all by 2 or 3 until they are. This reverses the usual process: normally the equation gives you the ratio, but here the experiment gives you the ratio and you write the equation.

bullets: **Limiting reactant**: the reactant that is completely used up and so limits the amount of products formed.
**Excess reactant**: the reactant that is left over once the reaction has finished because there was more than needed.
The amount of product is **proportional to the moles of limiting reactant**, so doubling the limiting reactant doubles the product (if everything else is in excess).
Adding more of the excess reactant does **not** increase the amount of product.
Think of making sandwiches: with 10 slices of bread and 3 slices of cheese you can only make a limited number of sandwiches; cheese is limiting.
Using an excess of a cheaper or more easily recycled reactant is a deliberate choice in industry to make sure the expensive reactant is fully used.
Which reactant is limiting depends on the **moles and the equation ratio**, not simply on which has the smaller mass.
core.h: Excess and limiting reactants: the key ideas
core.p: In many real reactions, two reactants are **not** supplied in exactly the correct ratio. It is common to use an **excess** of one reactant so that **all of the other reactant is used up**. The reactant that is **completely used up** is called the **limiting reactant**, because it **limits the amount of product** that can form. Once the limiting reactant has all reacted the reaction stops, even though some of the other reactant (the one in excess) is still left over. The amount of product depends only on the limiting reactant, never on the one in excess.

bullets: Example: 4.8 g Mg (0.20 mol) and 7.3 g HCl (0.20 mol) for Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2.
Mg needs 2 mol HCl per mol, so 0.20 mol Mg needs 0.40 mol HCl, but only 0.20 mol HCl is available, so **HCl is limiting**.
Divide by balancing number: Mg 0.20 ÷ 1 = 0.20; HCl 0.20 ÷ 2 = 0.10. The smaller (0.10) is HCl, confirming it is limiting.
Product: MgCl2 = ½ × 0.20 = 0.10 mol, mass = 0.10 × 95 = 9.5 g.
Mg used = 0.10 mol = 2.4 g, so 2.4 g of Mg is left over (the excess): 4.8 − 2.4 = 2.4 g.
Always state which reactant is limiting in words; examiners often award a mark for this.
Common trap: the reactant with the smaller **mass** is not automatically the limiting one.
core.h: Identifying the limiting reactant by calculation (Higher tier)
core.p: To decide which reactant is limiting, convert the mass of **each** reactant to moles, then compare with the ratio in the balanced equation. A reliable method is to **work out how much of the second reactant the first would need**. If you have more than that, the first is limiting; if you have less, the second is limiting. Equivalent method: divide the moles of each reactant by its balancing number; the **smaller result** is the limiting reactant. Then use the moles of the limiting reactant, never the excess one, to calculate the mass of product.

bullets: The **sloping section**: the reactant being added is limiting; product increases in direct proportion.
The **kink (change of gradient)** marks the exact point where the two reactants are in the ratio shown by the equation.
The **plateau**: the fixed reactant is limiting; the added reactant is now in excess.
Read the mass at the kink to find the moles of reactant needed for the fixed amount of the other, and use it to check the equation ratio.
The height of the plateau gives the maximum mass of product from the fixed reactant.
If you repeat with double the fixed reactant, the plateau is twice as high and the kink is twice as far along.
In an exam you may be asked to **sketch** this shape or to describe it in terms of limiting reactants.
core.p: A graph of **mass (or volume) of product against the amount of one reactant added**, with the other reactant fixed, has a distinctive shape. At first the graph is a **straight line through the origin**, because the added reactant is the limiting reactant and each extra bit makes a proportional amount of extra product. Then it reaches a **plateau** (horizontal line) at the point where the added reactant has used up all the fixed reactant. After that, the fixed reactant is limiting, so adding more of the first reactant makes no more product.

bullets: Excess insoluble solid + acid: the solid stops dissolving and sits at the bottom, showing the acid has all reacted.
Filtering removes the excess solid, leaving only the salt solution (then evaporate and crystallise).
In the Haber process an excess of cheap nitrogen can push the reaction to use up more hydrogen.
Burning fuel with **excess oxygen** ensures complete combustion and avoids carbon monoxide and soot.
A gas syringe experiment with excess metal ensures all the acid is used, so the gas volume depends only on the acid.
Using an excess is a design decision linked to cost, safety and purity of the product.
In a titration, the endpoint is when the limiting amount has exactly reacted with the other (equivalence point).
core.h: Why an excess is used in practice
core.p: Chemists often deliberately add one reactant in **excess** to make sure the other, more valuable or harder to separate reactant is completely used. In preparing a soluble salt, for example, an insoluble solid (metal, metal oxide, hydroxide or carbonate) is added to the acid until **no more reacts**, so the **acid is the limiting reactant**. The unreacted solid is easy to remove by **filtration**, leaving a pure salt solution. If the acid were in excess, the leftover acid would contaminate the salt and be difficult to remove.

bullets: Burning Mg in an open crucible: mass increases because oxygen atoms from the air join the magnesium.
Heating CaCO3 in an open tube: mass decreases because CO2 gas escapes.
Acid + carbonate in an open flask: mass decreases as CO2 escapes; in a sealed flask with a balloon it stays constant.
Always look for a gas in the equation to explain a mass change.
Explain with the phrase: 'the mass of the gas is not included in the measurement' (or 'the gas is included in the mass').
Calculations can find the mass of gas released: mass of gas = mass before − mass after (open system).
A common practical: heating copper carbonate and measuring the loss in mass to find the mass of CO2.
core.h: Apparent changes in mass during reactions
core.p: Sometimes the measured mass of a reaction mixture **appears to change** even though mass is conserved. This happens when a **gas is a reactant or product** and the container is **open**. When magnesium burns in air, it combines with oxygen from the air, so the solid product MgO has a **greater mass** than the Mg you started with. When calcium carbonate is heated, carbon dioxide gas escapes into the air so the mass of solid **decreases**. In a **sealed (closed) system** the total mass stays exactly the same, which proves the law.

bullets: Write the equation first; it earns a mark in its own right in many mark schemes.
Write each step on a new line with units: 'moles Mg = 6.0 ÷ 24 = 0.25 mol'.
Give the final answer with units (g, mol or tonne) and to a suitable number of significant figures.
Use standard form where the numbers are very large or small, e.g. 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol.
Show the Mr calculation: ‘Mr = 24 + 16 = 40’.
Check: total mass of products = total mass of reactants.
If your answer is larger than the total mass of reactants available, re-check the ratio.
core.h: Presenting calculations: units, significant figures and checks
core.p: Marks in calculation questions are given for **method, correct values and the final answer with units**, so a neat layout pays off. Give the answer to the **same number of significant figures as the data in the question** (usually 2 or 3), unless told otherwise. Do not round during the working; round only at the end. If the question gives you ‘relative atomic masses’ use them exactly. A final reasonableness check, such as 'Is the product mass similar to the reactant mass?' and 'Do the products add up to the reactants?', catches most errors before you move on.

bullets: Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100; the theoretical yield comes from the method in this note.
Atom economy = (Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all reactants) × 100.
Concentration: moles = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume (dm³), then use the equation ratio.
Gas volumes (triple, Higher): volume (dm³) = moles × 24 at room temperature and pressure.
Extraction of metals: the mass of iron from iron(III) oxide uses the ratio 1 : 2.
Neutralisation and titration: finding unknown concentrations from equation ratios.
Energy changes and rates questions often start from a reacting-mass calculation.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: Reacting mass calculations are the foundation of the rest of quantitative chemistry. **Percentage yield** compares the actual mass obtained with the theoretical mass calculated here. **Atom economy** uses Mr values of reactants and products from the same equation. **Concentration calculations** and **titrations** use moles = concentration × volume together with the same equation ratios. **Gas volume calculations** (Higher tier, chemistry-only) use 24 dm³ per mole at room temperature and pressure. In electrolysis and metal extraction, reacting masses tell you how much metal you can obtain from an ore.

exam: Command words: **calculate** means work out a numerical answer showing steps; **explain** needs a reason using the idea of limiting reactant or conservation of mass; **determine** means use data to reach a conclusion.
Typical 1-mark questions: state the Mr, state which reactant is in excess, or complete a balanced equation.
Typical 2-mark questions: work out moles from mass, or the mass of a product from a ratio; 1 mark for the method, 1 for the answer.
3-4 mark calculation: expect Mr (1), moles of known (1), ratio (1), mass of wanted with unit (1).
Model phrase for limiting reactant: 'X is the limiting reactant because it is completely used up, so no more product can form'.
Model phrase for excess: 'Y is in excess because there is more than needed to react with all of X, so some is left over'.
For mass changes: 'the mass increases because oxygen from the air combines with the magnesium' or 'mass decreases because carbon dioxide gas escapes'.
6-mark questions often combine a calculation with an explanation; plan: equation, Mr, moles, ratio, mass, then comment on the result.
Graph questions: describe the straight line (proportional), the change in gradient (limiting reactant changes) and the plateau (reaction has stopped because one reactant is used up).
Always check the final answer is sensible: product mass should not exceed the total reactant mass.
If you cannot finish, still write the equation and the Mr values: these earn marks on their own.

mistakes.r: Convert to moles first; the balancing numbers give a ratio of moles, and the masses depend on Mr.
mistakes.w: Using the balancing numbers as a ratio of masses (e.g. '2Mg gives 2MgO so 6 g gives 6 g').

mistakes.r: Reacting mass = Mr × balancing number, e.g. 2MgO is 2 × 40 = 80 g.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to multiply Mr by the balancing number when using the reacting-mass ratio.

mistakes.r: Use the Mr of the formula as written; diatomic elements are H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2, I2.
mistakes.w: Using the wrong Mr, e.g. O instead of O2 (16 not 32) or Cl instead of Cl2.

mistakes.r: The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first, found by comparing moles with the equation ratio.
mistakes.w: Saying the limiting reactant is the one with the smaller mass.

mistakes.r: Always use the moles of the limiting reactant, because it decides how much product forms.
mistakes.w: Using the moles of the excess reactant to find the mass of product.

mistakes.r: The mass of the solid decreases because the gas (e.g. CO2) escapes; the total mass of all substances is conserved.
mistakes.w: Saying 'mass is lost' when a gas escapes, as if atoms were destroyed.

mistakes.r: Keep full calculator values and round only the final answer; use Cl = 35.5.
mistakes.w: Rounding too early (e.g. Cl = 35 or moles to 1 s.f.) so the answer is wrong.

mistakes.r: Mass in g, amount in mol; include units in the final answer.
mistakes.w: Omitting units or writing 'mol' for a mass.

mistakes.r: Only change the balancing numbers; never alter the formula of a substance.
mistakes.w: Changing subscripts when balancing (e.g. writing MgO2).

summary: You must be able to use a balanced symbol equation to calculate the masses of reactants and products (and, at Higher tier, to balance equations from masses), and to explain and calculate the effect of a limiting reactant on the amount of product. This matters because it lets chemists predict yields, avoid waste and decide which reactant to use in excess.

terms.d: An equation showing the formulae of reactants and products with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.
The large number in front of a formula showing the relative number of moles of that substance in the equation.
No atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction, so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.
The average mass of an atom of an element compared with one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula.
The unit of amount of substance; one mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles.
The quantity, measured in moles, of a chemical.
A substance that is used up (present at the start) in a chemical reaction.
A substance that is made in a chemical reaction.
A reactant that is left over after the reaction has finished because more was added than needed.
The reactant that is completely used up in a reaction and so limits the amount of products formed.
A system in which no matter can enter or leave, so the mass stays the same.
The maximum mass of product that could be formed, calculated from the equation and the limiting reactant.
The ratio of moles of reactants and products shown by the balancing numbers.
The digits in a number that carry meaning, counted from the first non-zero digit.

worked.ans: 10 g of magnesium oxide (check: 6 g Mg + 4 g O = 10 g).
worked.q: Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. Calculate the mass of magnesium oxide formed when 6.0 g of magnesium burns completely. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16) [3 marks]
steps: Ratio 2 : 2, so moles of MgO = 0.25 mol.

worked.q: 4.8 g of magnesium reacts with 7.3 g of hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2. (Ar: Mg = 24, H = 1, Cl = 35.5) (a) Which reactant is limiting? (b) Calculate the mass of magnesium chloride formed. [5 marks]
steps: Moles Mg = 4.8 ÷ 24 = 0.20 mol. Mr HCl = 36.5, moles HCl = 7.3 ÷ 36.5 = 0.20 mol.
Mg needs 2 × 0.20 = 0.40 mol HCl but only 0.20 mol is available, so HCl is limiting.
Extra: Mg used = 0.10 mol = 2.4 g, so 2.4 g Mg is left over.

worked.q: 5.4 g of aluminium reacts with 21.3 g of chlorine to form 26.7 g of aluminium chloride. Use the masses to write the balanced equation. (Ar: Al = 27, Cl = 35.5) [4 marks, Higher tier]
steps: Moles Al = 5.4 ÷ 27 = 0.20 mol; moles Cl2 = 21.3 ÷ 71 = 0.30 mol.
